unit-weight: The weight of one cubic metre of a soil, in kN/m³, written γ. Damp sand weighs about 18 kN/m³; soaked, with water in every gap, about 20; water itself 9.81.
buoyant-unit-weight: The weight of a cubic metre of soaked soil less the weight of the water it displaces: γ′ = γsat − γw, about 10 kN/m³ for sand. Below a still water table it is how much each extra metre of depth adds to the grains' press.
strength-envelope: A plot of a soil's shear strength against its effective stress. For sand it is a straight line through zero rising at the friction angle, τ = σ′ tan φ′; a soil with cohesion starts the line at c′. Points below the line hold; none can lie above it.
infinite-slope: A slope so long and even that every part of its face is like every other, so one slab or one grain parallel to the face stands for the whole. For a sand with no cohesion it stands at the friction angle dry or under still water, and at tan β = (γ′/γsat) tan φ′ with water seeping out parallel to its face.
heave: The lifting of the ground when water flowing up through it pushes on the grains as hard as their buoyant weight presses down, at about the critical gradient; the grains stop pressing on one another and the surface rises or boils.

entry: The upward hydraulic gradient at which the drag of the flowing water equals the buoyant weight of the grains: i_c = γ′/γw, about 1.0 for sand. The grains stop pressing on one another, the effective stress is zero, and the sand heaves or boils.

The steepest slope at which one surface can rest on another without sliding, written φ; for a soil, measured against effective stress, φ′. Its tangent is the fraction of the press that friction can offer, so strength = effective stress × tan φ′. About 30–40° for sand.
